planting.note: Set divisions or container plants into well-drained soil in light to dappled shade; cut old foliage to the ground in late winter so the spring flowers show clearly.

directions: Thunderbolt is a selection of colchicum barrenwort valued for its bright green spring foliage that turns aubergine-purple in autumn while the leaf veins stay green, giving a jagged lightning-bolt pattern. Small yellow, flat-faced flowers open in early spring just before the new leaves unfurl. It tolerates sand, clay, and dry shade once established, making it a dependable groundcover under trees where watering is inconsistent. Shear old foliage to the ground in late winter so the emerging flowers are not hidden by the previous season's growth.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in a site shaded from hot afternoon sun; sun or shade shifts flower tone only slightly, soil pH shifts it more.

directions: Little Geisha is an unusual mountain hydrangea in that it carries rounded mophead flower clusters rather than the flat lacecap heads typical of the species, opening light pink or light blue depending on soil acidity. Its compact, rounded habit stays smaller than most bigleaf hydrangeas, making it a good choice for borders or containers where space is limited. Give it light to open shade protected from hot sun, consistently moist humus-rich soil, and only light pruning, since heavy cutbacks remove the next year's flower buds. Acidic Pacific Northwest soils push the color toward blue-purple; adding lime shifts it toward pink over a couple of seasons.

planting.note: Plant in rich, moist to well-drained soil in light to open shade sheltered from hot afternoon sun; avoid hard pruning, which sacrifices the next season's old-wood flower buds.

directions: Merritt's Beauty is a mophead bigleaf hydrangea grown for intensely saturated flower color, ranging from true blue to deep rose-red depending on soil pH, that covers the rounded shrub in early-to-mid summer. The bold, dense flowerheads read as a strong focal point in the summer garden, especially when massed or paired with silver or variegated foliage that sets off the color. Grow it in light to open shade with protection from hot sun, rich moist soil, and regular summer watering, since bigleaf hydrangeas are not drought tolerant. Limit pruning to removing a few old twiggy stems each year, since heavy cutbacks reduce flowering the following season.

planting.note: Plant container stock shallowly in rich, well-drained or sandy soil, since rhododendrons are shallow-rooted and resent deep planting; mulch to keep roots cool and moist.

directions: Capistrano is prized as one of the few reliable soft-yellow-flowered rhododendrons for maritime Northwest gardens, carrying frilly-edged, funnel-shaped pastel yellow blooms in dome-shaped trusses in mid-spring. It holds its leaves for two to three years rather than dropping them annually, which builds the dense, mounding habit that makes it useful as a structural evergreen even when not in bloom. Grow it in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light or open shade, and water regularly since rhododendrons are shallow-rooted and dry out quickly in summer heat. Pinch young growth to encourage bushiness and remove faded flower clusters for a tidier look.

planting.note: Set divisions into average garden soil in light to dappled shade; cut old foliage back in late winter before the flower stems and new leaves emerge.

directions: Cupreum carries dainty rose-and-coral flowers with lemon-yellow center cups on wiry stems above bronze-red new foliage that matures to green and colors again in fall. The delicate appearance belies a tough, long-lived plant that tolerates a wide range of soils from sand to clay and shrugs off summer drought once established. Grow it in light to dappled shade, where flowering and foliage color are best; it will also persist in deeper shade with reduced bloom. Shear the previous year's leaves to the ground in late winter so the new flowers and foliage are not obscured.

planting.note: Plant container stock in rich, well-drained soil in light to open shade; cut old leaves to the ground in December or early January to display the flowers.

directions: HGC Merlin is a hybrid hellebore from a German breeding program, bred for flowers held well above the foliage on sturdy stems rather than nodding at ground level as in many older hellebores. Light pink buds open and mature to a dusky rose over a long late-winter display, set against dark green, disease-resistant evergreen leaves. Plant in rich, well-drained soil in light to open shade and water at least weekly during dry spells. Cut the old foliage to the ground in early winter so the flowers are fully visible, then trim spent blooms back in late spring.

planting.note: Plant container stock in rich, well-drained soil in light to open shade; cut old leaves to the ground in December or early January to display the flowers.

directions: HGC Monte Cristo pairs blue-gray evergreen foliage with creamy flowers washed in soft peach and green tones through late winter, giving a cooler, more muted look than pink- or red-flowered hellebore hybrids. The disease-resistant leaves stay attractive most of the year but are best cut to the ground in early winter so the flower display takes center stage. Grow it in rich, well-drained soil in light to open shade, watering at least weekly during dry weather since hellebores do not thrive if allowed to dry out repeatedly. Group several plants together for the best effect in a winter woodland planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions in rich, well-drained soil in light to open shade; keep consistently moist, especially through the first growing season.

directions: Tracy's maidenhair is a West Coast native fern with dainty, triangular, bright green fronds carried on wiry black stems, giving it the airy, delicate look typical of maidenhair ferns. It stays evergreen to semi-evergreen in mild winters but can look ragged by late winter in colder gardens, which is the best time to cut the old fronds back before new growth emerges. Grow it in rich, well-drained soil in light to dappled shade with consistent moisture, stepping up watering during hot or dry spells since this fern does not tolerate prolonged drought. It is a good companion for other small-scale woodland perennials along a shaded path or rock garden.

planting.note: Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in open to dappled shade; cut fronds to the ground in late winter before new growth emerges.

directions: Dyce's holly fern is a large, robust evergreen fern that forms a vase-shaped bouquet of glossy, dark green fronds, lending bold texture to a shaded border without crowding out neighboring plants. It is substantial enough to stand alone as an accent in a small garden or to be massed for a dramatic effect in a larger woodland planting. Give it humus-rich, well-drained soil in open to dappled shade and water regularly to frequently during dry periods, since it is not as drought tolerant as some other Polystichum species. Cut the fronds to the ground in late winter, just before the new growth begins to unfurl, to keep the clump looking fresh.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in rich, well-drained soil in light to open shade; martagon hybrids are slow to settle in and may take a couple of seasons before flowering well.

directions: Arabian Knight is a martagon hybrid lily whose recurved, Turk's-cap-shaped petals open in mahogany to burnt-umber tones edged in gold, with centers speckled rust-red, carried in whorls up tall leafy stems in summer. It thrives in light to open shade better than most lilies, making it a good choice for a dappled woodland border rather than open sun. Plant bulbs in fall in rich, well-drained soil and expect a slow but worthwhile establishment, since martagon types can take a couple of years to settle in before flowering reliably. Once established, clumps are long-lived and will naturalize in a favorable site; watch for slugs on the emerging spring shoots.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in rich, well-drained soil in light to open shade; martagon hybrids are slow to settle in and may take a couple of seasons before flowering well.

directions: Claude Shride is a martagon hybrid lily with striking dark maroon, recurved petals rimmed in a thin orange edge and flecked with orange, set off by prominent rusty-orange anthers. Like other martagons it carries whorled flowers up tall leafy stems in summer and performs best in light to open shade rather than full sun. Plant bulbs in fall in rich, well-drained or sandy soil; growth is slow at first, but established clumps bloom reliably for many years and can naturalize where conditions suit them. Cut stems to the ground in autumn once the foliage yellows, and protect emerging shoots from slugs and snails in spring.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in rich, well-drained soil in light to open shade; martagon hybrids are slow to settle in and may take a couple of seasons before flowering well.

directions: Manitoba Morning is a shorter martagon hybrid lily, its recurved petals shaded rose with hints of orange and scattered burgundy speckles, accented by prominent rusty-orange anthers. The whorled summer flowers are carried on stems generally under four feet, making it easier to fit into a smaller woodland bed than taller martagon cultivars. Plant bulbs in fall in rich, well-drained soil in light to open shade; expect slow establishment but a long-lived, naturalizing clump once settled. Water regularly during dry weather and watch for slugs on the tender spring shoots.

planting.note: Plant shallowly in rich, well-drained or sandy soil in light to open shade; water weekly or more often in dry spells since rhododendrons are shallow-rooted.

directions: Golfer is grown chiefly as a foliage rhododendron: its oval leaves emerge coated in a glowing silvery-white indumentum that gradually recedes over the growing season to reveal dark green foliage beneath. Pink buds open to white flowers flushed pink in spring, but the bloom is a secondary feature compared to the striking new growth. Grow it in rich, well-drained or sandy soil in light to open shade, with regular watering since it is shallow-rooted like other rhododendrons. Remove faded flower clusters for a tidier appearance through the season.

planting.note: Plant shallowly in rich, well-drained or sandy soil in light to open shade; this species is grown primarily for its felted foliage rather than its flowers.

directions: Rhododendron pachysanthum, a species originally collected in Taiwan's high mountains, is one of the finest foliage rhododendrons for the garden, its arrowhead-shaped leaves coated on both sides in a woolly felt, called indumentum, that ranges from near-white to tawny fawn as it emerges. Over the growing season the indumentum on the upper leaf surface wears away to reveal glossy dark green foliage, giving the plant changing texture and color year-round. White flowers flushed pink appear in spring but take a back seat to the foliage display. Grow it in rich, well-drained or sandy soil in light to open shade with regular watering, since its shallow roots dry out quickly in summer heat.

planting.note: Give this large-leaved rhododendron plenty of room and plant shallowly in rich, well-drained or sandy soil in light to open shade; site where low afternoon or evening sun can light up the colored leaf undersides.

directions: Sir Charles Lemon is grown mainly for its large, dark green leaves, whose undersides are richly colored in fulvous orange-brown to rust tones that glow when backlit by low sun. White flowers appear in spring but are a secondary attraction next to the foliage. This is a substantial, eventually tree-like shrub that needs considerable room to reach its mature size, so site it where its spread will not be a problem. Grow it in rich, well-drained or sandy soil in light to open shade with regular watering, and position it so that evening sun can catch the colorful leaf undersides.

planting.note: Plant shallowly in rich, well-drained or sandy soil in light to open shade; this yakushimanum-type hybrid stays compact, making it suitable for smaller gardens.

directions: Yaku Prince is a yakushimanum-type hybrid rhododendron with deep rose buds that open pink and mature to white flushed pink, set against evergreen foliage coated in a colorful woolly indumentum. The silvery-white felt on the upper leaf surface recedes over the season, while a tawny coating persists underneath, giving year-round foliage interest beyond the spring bloom. Its compact, dense habit, inherited from R. yakushimanum, makes it well suited to smaller shaded gardens where larger rhododendrons would overwhelm the space. Grow it in rich, well-drained or sandy soil in light to open shade with regular watering during dry weather.

planting.note: Plant shallowly in rich, well-drained or sandy soil in light to open shade; this yakushimanum-type hybrid stays compact, making it suitable for smaller gardens.

directions: Yaku Princess is a yakushimanum-type hybrid rhododendron with deep pink buds that open pink and fade to white, carried above evergreen foliage covered in a woolly, silvery-white felt when new that turns tawny underneath as it matures. Its dense, mounding habit, derived from R. yakushimanum parentage, keeps the plant tidy and in scale with smaller shaded borders. Grow it in rich, well-drained or sandy soil in light to open shade and water regularly through dry spells, since rhododendrons are shallow-rooted. Remove spent flower trusses to keep the plant looking neat.

planting.note: Plant in loamy, well-drained soil with morning sun and afternoon shade for the best flowering and foliage condition.

directions: Seaview Sunset is a recent rhododendron selection known for flowers that blend soft apricot, peach, and golden-yellow tones, often tinged pink, producing a warm sunset-like display in mid-to-late spring. The compact, rounded evergreen habit and dark green foliage keep it in scale with smaller gardens or as a featured specimen near a patio. It performs best with morning sun and afternoon shade in loamy, well-drained soil, and needs regular to frequent watering since rhododendrons are shallow-rooted. Deadhead spent flower trusses to maintain a clean appearance through the season.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in well-drained soil in full sun to light or open shade; established clumps need only occasional watering.

directions: Alpine lady's mantle forms a low, compact mat of deeply lobed, silver-edged green leaves with a fine, silky sheen that catches and beads dewdrops and raindrops, a smaller-scale alternative to the larger, more commonly grown Alchemilla mollis. Airy sprays of tiny yellow-green flowers rise just above the foliage in summer, adding a soft textural accent rather than bold color. It is easygoing in well-drained soil in full sun to light or open shade, tolerating a wider range of light than many shade perennials. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to keep the mat tidy and vigorous.

planting.note: Plant container stock in organically rich, well-draining soil in light to open shade or morning sun with afternoon shade; a site sheltered from hard frost protects open winter flowers.

directions: Yume, whose name means 'dream' in Japanese, bears soft, peony-form flowers that blend white, blush pink, and pale lavender for an ethereal, watercolor effect. It typically begins flowering as early as November and continues into January, giving color through the darkest months when few other shrubs are in bloom. Grow it in organically rich, well-draining soil in light to open shade or with morning sun and afternoon shade, and water regularly through the dry season, especially in late summer, to support strong bud set. A sheltered spot near a wall or building helps protect the winter flowers from hard frost.
